mcqs.question: According to the answer skeleton, which factor alone can make a monolith the better choice?
options: The team doesn't yet have any engineers experienced with Kubernetes
The company hasn't hired a dedicated platform team yet
The product hasn't been publicly launched yet
In-process latency matters more than independent deployability, even if the team could separate the domain cleanly
mcqs.explanation: The skeleton names three independently sufficient reasons: small team, an unclear domain split, or latency mattering more than independent deploys — that third one holds even if the domain actually could be cleanly separated. Missing platform expertise or launch status aren't part of the actual criteria.

mcqs.question: A pre-product-market-fit startup redesigns its core domain model every few weeks. Why is this a strong argument against microservices right now?
options: Splitting into microservices now would mean renegotiating service boundaries and API contracts on the same weekly cadence, far more expensive than refactoring inside one codebase
Microservices technically cannot support any domain model that changes over time
Investors generally view microservices as a sign of premature scaling
The startup doesn't have enough traffic yet to need multiple servers
mcqs.explanation: The cost is specifically about coordination: a fast-changing domain model means service boundaries drawn today are likely wrong next month, and fixing that across services (versioned API changes, coordinated deploys) costs far more than the same fix inside one codebase. It's not a technical impossibility, an investor-perception issue, or purely about traffic volume.

mcqs.question: The team that started at 5 people is now 50. Has the microservices calculus changed?
options: Likely yes — a shared monolith now blocks 50 engineers on one release train, a cost that has grown larger than the network-hop cost microservices would add
No — team size never changes whether a monolith or microservices is the right architecture
Only if the company also expands into a new product line
No — the domain's separability, not team size, is the only factor that matters
mcqs.explanation: The calculus is a genuine cost comparison, not a fixed rule: at 50 people, the monolith's shared release train and unclear code ownership become a real, growing cost, which can now outweigh the network-hop cost that made a monolith the right call at 5 people. Team size is one of the three factors in the skeleton, alongside domain separability and latency needs — not irrelevant, and not the only one.

mcqs.question: A 6-person team adopts microservices because "that's what companies like Netflix and Amazon do." What's the actual flaw in this reasoning?
options: Netflix and Amazon's architectures are outdated and no longer represent best practice
Microservices require a specific programming language those companies also use
Those companies adopted microservices to solve a scale problem — a shared release train blocking hundreds of engineers — that a 6-person team doesn't have yet
Small companies are legally required to use simpler architectures
mcqs.explanation: The flaw is copying an architectural choice without the problem that motivated it: those companies split services to solve a real bottleneck at their scale, which a 6-person team simply doesn't have. This isn't about the architecture being outdated, a language requirement, or any legal constraint.
